title: The derivative as a limit
note: The derivative f′(a) is the limit of secant slopes (f(a + h) − f(a))/h as h → 0. It is the slope of the tangent line and the instantaneous rate of change. A function can be continuous yet fail to have a derivative at a corner, a cusp, or a vertical tangent.

read.title: From secant to tangent
text: Pick two points on a curve, x = a and x = a + h, and draw the line through them. Its slope, (f(a + h) − f(a))/h, is the average rate of change of f over that stretch. Now slide the second point toward the first by shrinking h. The secant lines pivot and settle on a single line that just touches the curve at a: the tangent line. Its slope is the limit of the secant slopes, and that limit is the derivative f′(a).
For f(x) = x², the secant slope at x is ((x + h)² − x²)/h = (2xh + h²)/h = 2x + h. As h shrinks to 0 this becomes 2x, so the slope of the parabola at any x is 2x.

The same number has a physical meaning. If s(t) is position, the secant slope is average velocity over a time interval, and the derivative is instantaneous velocity. Differentiating again gives acceleration.

A derivative needs the curve to look like a line when you zoom in. At a corner, as in |x| at 0, the secant slopes from the left and right approach different values, so no single tangent exists, even though the graph is unbroken.
